'''Weyto''' (also called '''Wayto''') is a speculative [[extinct language]] thought to have been spoken in the [[Lake Tana]] region of [[Ethiopia]] by the [[Weyto caste|Weyto]], a small group of [[hippopotamus]] hunters who now speak [[Amharic language|Amharic]]. 

== History ==
The Weyto language was first mentioned by the Scottish traveler [[James Bruce]], who spoke Amharic. Bruce passed through the area about 1770 and reported that "the Weyto speak a language radically different from any of those in [[Abyssinia]]," but was unable to obtain any "certain information" on it, despite prevailing upon the king to send for two Weyto men for him to ask questions, which they would "neither answer nor understand" even when threatened with hanging. 

The next European to report on the Weyto, [[Eugen Mittwoch]], described them as uniformly speaking a dialect of Amharic.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mittwoch |first=Eugen |url=https://books.google.com/books?vid=PRNC:32101073503300 |title=Mittheilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen an der Königlichen Friedrich Wilhelms-Universität zu Berlin |date=1907 |publisher=Commissionsverlag von W. Spemann |pages=185–241 |language=de |chapter=Proben aus dem amharischen Volksmund}}</ref> This report was confirmed by [[Marcel Griaule]] when he passed through in 1928, although he added that at one point a Weyto sang an unrecorded song "in the dead language of the Wohitos" whose meaning the singer himself did not understand, except for a handful of words for hippopotamus body parts which, he says, had remained in use.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Griaule |first=Marcel |title=Les flambeurs d'hommes |date=1991 |publisher=Berg International |isbn=978-2-900269-76-3 |edition=Repr |series=Territoires de l'autre |location=Paris}}</ref>

== Classification ==
The paucity of the data available has not prevented speculation on the classification of their original language. Cohen suggested that it might have been either an [[Agaw languages|Agaw language]] or a non-Amharic [[Semitic language]], while Dimmendaal (1989) says it "probably belonged to Cushitic" (as does Agaw),<ref>{{Citation |last=Dimmendaal |first=Gerrit J. |title=On language death in eastern Africa |date=1989-07-06 |work=Investigating Obsolescence |pages=13–32 |editor-last=Dorian |editor-first=Nancy C. |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/CBO9780511620997A012/type/book_part |access-date=2026-05-08 |edition=1 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/cbo9780511620997.005 |isbn=978-0-521-32405-2}}</ref> and Gamst (1965) says "...it can be assumed that if the Wäyto did not speak Amharic 200 years ago, their language must have been Agäw..."<ref name=":0" /> According to the ''[[Ethnologue]]'', Bender ''et al.'' (1976) saw it as Cushitic,<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_194361020 |title=Language in Ethiopia |date=1976 |publisher=Oxford Univ. Press |isbn=978-0-19-436102-6 |editor-last=Bender |editor-first=Marvin Lionel |series=Ford Foundation language surveys |location=London}}</ref> while Bender (1983) saw it as either [[Eastern Sudanic languages|Eastern Sudanic]] or [[Awngi language|Awngi]].<ref>{{Cite book |last= |title=Nilo-Saharan language studies |date=1983 |publisher=[[Summer Institute of Linguistics]] |editor-last=Bender |editor-first=M. L. |location=Dallas, Texas}}</ref>

==Vocabulary==
This Amharic dialect is described by [[Marcel Cohen]] (1939) as featuring a fair number of words derived from Amharic roots but twisted in sound or meaning in order to confuse outsiders, making it a sort of [[argot]]. In addition, the dialect had a small number of [[Cushitic languages|Cushitic]] [[loanword]]s not found in standard Amharic, and a large number of [[Arabic language|Arabic]] loanwords mainly related to [[Islam]]. Of the substantial wordlist collected by Griaule, Cohen only considered six terms to be etymologically obscure: ''šəlkərít'' "fish-scale", ''qəntat'' "wing", ''čəgəmbit'' "mosquito", ''annessa'' "shoulder", ''<sup>ə</sup>nk<sup>i</sup>es'' "hippopotamus thigh", ''wazəməs'' "hippopotamus spine." By 1965, the visiting anthropologist [[Frederick Gamst]] found "no surviving native words, not even relating to their hunting and fishing work tasks."<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Gamst |first=Frederick C. |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/Travel_and_Research_in_Northwestern_Ethi.html?id=5JoPAQAAMAAJ&redir_esc=y |title=Travel and Research in Northwestern Ethiopia |date=1965 |publisher=Institute of Ethiopian Studies, Haile Sellassie I University |language=en}}</ref>
